docs.title: Sankhara
docs.text:
Sankhara follows a people from a small band at their first fires to whatever they become, lived one person at a time. Each turn is a year. You act as one character, with a few slots of attention and the means your place among the people gives you: what is held in common if you lead, your family's if you hunt, gather or keep the songs. Some things take years; events arrive, some of them asking something of you.

The ideas behind it are in Concepts; how they are built is in Architecture.

Status

Playable: a band of a few hundred people, yearly turns, multi-year undertakings you can let run, a web of discoveries whose forms the people settle on, roles that appear as the people change, and other peoples to meet. Policy and more development come in Milestone 2; detailed NPC relationships and politics in Milestone 3.

docs.title: Running
docs.text:
uv sync
uv run sankhara        # or: uv run python -m sankhara

Choose New Game. Click a slot under Your attention to decide what the year is for, then End the Year, or Let the years pass to keep going until something needs you. The game saves itself every year; Continue picks up where you left off.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
All code lives in the sankhara package under src/. The game is split into a pure-Python simulation (sankhara.sim, no Kivy, fully unit-tested and saveable) and a UI (sankhara.ui) that only reads state and calls a handful of game functions.

Package Responsibility sankhara.sim The game: state, rules, the yearly loop, lives and save/load. sankhara.world Map generation (map_gen.py) and hex-grid math (hexgrid.py). sankhara.core game_engine.generate_map(seed) builds the terrain. sankhara.entities Name generation per culture (namer.py). sankhara.ui Kivy screens: menu, game view (with the chooser, "What we know" and the choice of a custom's form), between-lives screen; theme.py palette and widgets; words.py turns numbers into the words the player sees. sankhara.constants config.py: map size, noise, biome thresholds and resources, culture groups. sankhara.app SankharaApp: screen flow and autosave.

docs.title: How the design maps to code
docs.text:
The design lives in Concepts. After the first play-through the game starts with a small band rather than a kingdom; this is how that is built:

Design Implementation One turn is one year game.end_year() advances the world one year, then begin_year() sets up the next. 2–3 slots of personal attention stations.ACTION_SLOTS = 3. A slot holds a one-year deed (actions.py), an answer to an obligation, or a multi-year project (projects.py). Lead from wherever you are Most projects are the people's works (Project.common). Anyone can begin one with their own means (at half cost; slower), help with one someone else leads (each helper adds work), take up one left unfinished, or call others to it (rally: spends standing to add support, which adds work and draws NPC helpers). NPCs join works more readily when the one leading is respected or liked. When a leader dies or sets a work aside it passes to a helper, the people's leader or an elder (projects.pass_on), or waits for someone. A custom being settled lets anyone speak for a form; a respected voice weighs more (game.choose_form, pending_mode). The thread between lives Works an earlier character of the player's worked on stay in play: the birth screen lists what was finished while the new character grew up and what is still unfinished and who carries it (game.thread_lines), and the chooser marks those works. GameState.legacy remembers finished works and settled customs the player had a hand in; the end-of-life screen shows them. Multi-year projects, run until interrupted A Project keeps its slot year after year until finished, set aside or stalled. Its cost, tags and karma count every year it is worked. YearReport.interrupts lists what should stop "Let the years pass": an obligation, a finished or stalled project, a discovery, a choice to make, strangers, a death or birth in the family, a life ending. A coarse budget, no money at the start Budget is open-ended: food, hands (labour, renewed yearly) and regard (standing). The leader also draws on what is held in common. Exchange adds whatever form the people settle on (favours owed, wares, or tokens named for the land: shells, polished stones, beads). Costs for the common stores scale with the square root of the population. Start as the first band, not a civilisation game.new_game(): about 250 people in three camps, four known things (fire, stone edges, the old songs, a belief in the unseen whose form is random), a young leader whose mother has just died. Development like Civilization, but not prescribed discoveries.py: about 30 ideas in four domains (land, craft, lore, kin). One is available only when its prerequisites and circumstances hold (water nearby, grassland, game, having met another people, enough people). Insight comes from ordinary life every year, from someone working at it (the pursue project, one idea at a time), from chance events, and from other peoples. Ideas settle into forms Discoveries like customs of giving, planting, exchange, how leaders are chosen, or judgement have several forms with different effects (Form). The player chooses if they worked it out, or if they lead and it is a matter of custom. Otherwise the people's own inclinations decide. A choice strengthens its tags and weighs (lightly) on karma. Roles appear as the people change stations.py: leader, keeper, hunter, gatherer and maker at first; fisher, planter, herder and go-between appear with the discoveries that make them; hunters and gatherers grow rarer as herding and planting arrive. Rebirth draws from the roles that exist. How leaders are found can change people.next_leader(): the most respected at first; later a council of elders, the strongest, or a lineage, depending on the form "how the people decide" takes. Titles follow (nation.names). Other peoples; violence real but not the focus peoples.py: three other peoples, simulated coarsely. They grow, learn, meet you, share ideas, intermarry, and drift toward or away from you. Raids come as events; the obligation is to seek redress; avenging is a harsh alternative answer. No armies. Karma only on the action layer Deeds and projects carry a hidden karma for their intention; skipped obligations subtract EventInstance.penalty. Outcomes never touch it. Stored on Soul.karma, clamped to [-1, 1]. Lives of 20–50 turns, random death age Character.death_age is hidden: 16 + 20..50. Health can end a life sooner. Rebirth among the same people, random role game.begin_next_life(); childhood is fast-forwarded to age 16. Karma shapes conditions, not rank Carried-over inclinations, health, fortune, family stability, parents' warmth and which family you are born to. Half of it is spent doing so. Tendencies, felt not shown tendencies.py: choosing strengthens tags; declining a habitual default or setting a project aside weakens them. Inclinations change costs (±30%), order and tint in the chooser, and which deeds and projects are pre-filled in empty slots. NPCs, same model simplified npc.py: tracked adults take on projects (elders and the leader always) and a deed a year by inclination; the leader also by the people's needs. Their deeds earn standing; only the leader's act on the people. No win condition The game runs until the player stops; it autosaves every year.

docs.title: Simulation modules
docs.text:
• state.py: dataclasses (GameState, Nation, Settlement, Neighbour, Project, Character, Soul, Budget, EventInstance) with to_dict/from_dict. The RNG state is saved too, so a loaded game plays on identically.
  • game.py: founding the people, the options for a year, the yearly loop and its interrupts, choosing a custom's form, death and the next life.
  • discoveries.py: the web of ideas, their forms and combined effects, yearly insight.
  • projects.py: multi-year undertakings: working at ideas, ranging further, new camps, gathering places, store pits, fields, teaching, raising a child, apprentices, friendship and trade with other peoples...
  • actions.py: one-year deeds for each role, and the answers events ask for.
  • events.py: event definitions, yearly generation, obligation resolution (including alternative answers).
  • nation.py: each camp's food from its land (falling as it fills up), hunger and growth, what goes into the common stores, cohesion (which strains as the people grow), plenty and lore; each tracked family's means.
  • people.py: creating characters, families, ageing, marriage (sometimes to other peoples) and births, finding a new leader, keeping a few elders.
  • peoples.py, stations.py, tendencies.py, npc.py, world.py (cached map per seed, foraging values, place names), save.py (JSON).

docs.title: World generation
docs.text:
1. Perlin noise produces elevation and moisture grids of MAP_WIDTH × MAP_HEIGHT, sampled at each hex's true position and normalised to [0, 1]. The game seed fixes the map.
  2. Each value is bucketed by ELEVATION_THRESHOLDS / MOISTURE_THRESHOLDS; the pair names the biome (e.g. "Hill Forest").
  3. Resources are seeded from BIOME_RESOURCE_BASELINES; a tile's fertility (plant food, animal food, fresh water) drives harvests.

docs.title: Hex grid
docs.text: world/hexgrid.py is pure math for a pointy-top grid in "odd-r" offset coordinates: centres, exact pixel-to-tile picking, corners, neighbours, distance and fitting a map to a box. The map view dims land outside the people's range, outlines its border, marks camps (the leader's in saffron), outlines the player's home, and shows the ranges of other peoples once met.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text: The game's mechanics are meant to model a handful of Buddhist ideas. This page is a skeleton to be expanded from the original design conversation.

docs.title: Saṅkhāra
docs.text: Mental formations or volitional impulses: one of the five aggregates and the second link of dependent origination. In the game, the accumulated effect of a character's choices.

docs.title: Karma
docs.text: Intentional action and its consequences. Each turn's actions (and skipped obligations) adjust a karma score clamped to [-1, 1]; see ACTIONS in sankhara/constants/config.py.

docs.title: Rebirth and lineage
docs.text: A player is born into a Family on a home tile, which determines their culture group and names. Player.reincarnate() swaps in a new state (and optionally a new family); how karma drives rebirth is still to be designed.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• How karma maps to the next birth (species, family, location).
  • Whether NPCs share the same karma model.

docs.title: User Notes
docs.text:
• Original conversation is lost.
  • The game overall is supposed to be a nation builder that does not focus on war and army building. It's supposed to be a strategy game with resource mangament, policy/government management, scientific and cultural development but without armies and war being the main goal.
  • The Karma and rebirth cycle was inspired by the mechanics of the leader in games like Europa Universalis, in which the player is in charge of a country, but the leaders are born and die throughout the game, and lineage is an import aspect of holding power.

docs.title: Updated design direction:
docs.text:
Design summary

Premise. A nation builder with no focus on war or armies. Play centers on resource management, policy and government, and scientific and cultural development. Buddhist ideas (saṅkhāra, karma, rebirth) are modeled in the mechanics but never named or highlighted. There is no win condition, and the game runs until the player stops.

Turn structure. One turn is one year. The player acts as the current character, not as an abstract manager of the nation. Each turn has two layers: a fixed number of action slots (about 2 to 3) representing personal attention, and a coarse resource budget (a few categories) representing the nation’s capacity, which actions spend. Karma attaches only to the action layer: which actions are chosen and which obligations are skipped. Budget allocation affects the nation but not karma.

Events. Each year brings events, some random and some driven by the nation’s state. No attempt is made at fairness. Outcomes can be unjust or pointless. Events are the main source of obligations, and skipping them is penalized in karma. Karma tracks intention and choice, never outcomes.

Lifespan and lineage. A character’s life runs roughly 20 to 50 turns with a randomized death age, so the player cannot time final decisions. A full game spans several hundred turns and roughly 6 to 12 lives. Succession and lineage matter, as in Europa Universalis leaders.

Karma. Karma is a hidden score clamped to [-1, 1], never displayed as a number or label. Its only visible effects are felt ones.

Rebirth. Rebirth always stays within the same nation. Social station at rebirth is random, so players are not guaranteed to be rulers, and rank is not part of the karmic ledger at all. Every station has the same size of action set, with differing kinds and scopes of influence: a ruler’s is broad and slow, while a farmer’s or merchant’s is local and immediate. The design deliberately takes the position that status says nothing about worth. Karma governs the conditions within the station: mainly internal (tendencies), with smaller material (health, wealth within the station, family stability) and relational (parents, spouse, advisors, friends) adjustments. Becoming non-human is excluded from the main game, possibly reserved for an easter egg.

Tendencies (saṅkhāra). The past life’s habitual choices become the next life’s default impulses. They are never shown as labels or a character sheet and are only felt through the interface: some actions are cheaper in attention or resources, more prominent or tempting, or carry friction. The effect is a mild-to-moderate nudge that can always be overridden at a small extra cost. Effects must be consistent enough to be learnable. Tendencies shift throughout life at a constant rate: repetition strengthens them and acting against them weakens them, and the pattern at death is what carries into the next life.

NPCs. NPCs use the same model in simplified form, with tendencies that shift based on coarsely simulated choices. Rulers, heirs, advisors, and people near the player or in positions of power are tracked in detail, and the rest are handled statistically. Because rebirth stays in one nation, the people the player influenced remain, and the player can be reborn into the consequences of how they treated and shaped them.

docs.title: Updates after first play through (basic UI done from Milestone 1)
docs.text:
No descriptions of the game, including "about" sections or subtitles, should give away the "punchline" of their being "no winning". That's a huge spoiler, so it should never be explicit. Similarly, the karma mechanism should not be explicitly stated. Starting @ 20 is acceptable for now, but the civilization is far too advanced. It needs to start much further back without so many modern assumptions applied. There should not yet be coin money or "goods" to be traded. Imagine the first tribe of people that became modern humans that walked out of Africa, that's where you start, but not in Africa. It should be a small tribe, max 1,500, with no clear economic system, no farming, nothing but some oral traditions, superstitions/religius beleifs, names, language, but socially very early in their development. Currency, trade, cities, all of that needs to be discovered, designed, developed. But I don't want it to be prescribed as coming out the way things are now in the real world (e.g. coins, banks, etc.). This game should be more fluid than that, and play more like a simulation of human society over generations that a player can influence through their decisions. War is specifically deprioritized, so nothing about combat or armies to start, but that is something that will need to be addressed, becuase violence is real, and I want some aspects of it in the game. It can't be the focus, though.

A separate design effort needs to be made for the attention choices. They're okay to start, and as fillers, but this needs some close attention.

There should be multi-year projects with interupting events every few years, instead of having to manually choose minutia events each year. Similar to the mechanism in civilization with research, or building, or whatever taking a few turns, and if "auto end turn" is selected, the game runs the plan until something (e.g. disaster, other player) interrupts.

Much of the development mechanism should be like Civilization, which is an excellent game, but there's way too much of a focus on combat. The development mechanisms, though, are very good and should be thought of as a guide for Sankhara.

docs.title: Feedback 2
docs.text: Desicions at all levels of society that are under control of any station should show a clear, connected influence over the direction of society. The mechanics of the UI are generally okay, but the individual is taking too much focus over building the nation. The odds of becoming a leader are very small, so most of the game will likely be played as a farmer, which isn't quite the intent. I understand how mathematically there is simply a higher chance of being a farmer than a leader, since there are more farmers than leaders, but the game has to allow for players to lead from wherever they are. For example, the projects started in the first round when the player is the leader should still be relevant to the next character, like they can work on the project to build roads that the leader started, or something like that. The "a life begins" is a good place to keep that thread going.

docs.title: Development
docs.text:
Requires uv. The project is pinned to Python 3.12 (.python-version); uv will download it if needed.

uv sync                     # create .venv with runtime + dev dependencies
uv run pre-commit install   # run ruff and basic checks on every commit

docs.title: Common commands
docs.text: Task Command Run the game uv run sankhara Tests (with coverage) uv run pytest Lint uv run ruff check . Format uv run ruff format . All pre-commit hooks uv run pre-commit run --all-files Docs preview uv run --group docs mkdocs serve

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: Tests live in tests/, mirroring the package layout (test_core/, test_world/, …). tests/conftest.py sets KIVY_NO_ARGS so Kivy doesn't consume pytest's arguments. UI tests need a display; CI runs them under xvfb-run.

docs.title: CI
docs.text: GitHub Actions runs lint and tests on every push and pull request (.github/workflows/ci.yml), and publishes these docs to GitHub Pages on pushes to main (.github/workflows/docs.yml).
